bundle.name: San Francisco, wine country and the Monterey Bay coast: eight days worth stealing
bundle.description: Day-shaped playbooks from the three places a Northern California trip actually lives — the city, the Napa and Russian River valleys, and Highway 1 from Capitola to Big Sur. Built around the things that gate them: the Saturday market, the Alcatraz release window, appointment-only tastings you cannot drive yourself between, the Aquarium's first forty minutes, and the few winter weeks the Pfeiffer keyhole lights. Prices, booking rules and Highway 1 closures current for September 2026.
sources: PROVENANCE: mixed. The Sonoma, Capitola, Monterey and Big Sur days were researched against the sources below; the three San Francisco days and the Napa day were written without live web access and their prices need the same verification pass as the bundles marked above — see KI-2026-09-06-d.

playbooks.name: San Francisco: Ferry Plaza on a Saturday, the 11:00 boat to Alcatraz, crab in Chinatown
playbooks.summary: The market before the tour groups, a flat walk up the Embarcadero to Pier 33, the island in the middle of the day, and North Beach downhill into Chinatown for dinner. The whole shape of it hangs on one ticket bought three months ago.

sourceTrip.name: Bay Area, the long weekend that became a week

stops.title: Ferry Plaza Farmers Market, back plaza first
stops.notes: Saturday 08:00-14:00 is the big market — 100-plus vendors wrapping the whole building. Tuesday and Thursday are 10:00-14:00 and only in front, along the Embarcadero, which is the prepared-food half. So on a Saturday walk straight through the building to the BACK plaza over the water: that is where the actual farmers are. The front is where the tour groups queue. Get there before 09:00 or the Roli Roti porchetta line is 25 minutes on its own.

stops.title: Inside the Ferry Building for coffee and things to carry
stops.notes: Acme bread and Cowgirl Creamery are the two counters worth carrying something out of. Do not eat a proper lunch here — you want to be hungry in North Beach at 14:45, and Hog Island at noon is a 40-minute wait for the same oysters you can get at 11:00 on a weekday.

stops.title: Walk the Embarcadero north to Pier 33
stops.notes: 1.4 flat miles past Pier 7 and the historic F-line. Do not drive: Pier 33 parking is $40-plus for the day and the streetcar takes as long as walking because it shares the road. Boarding closes 15 minutes before departure and they genuinely do not hold the boat — a missed sailing is a forfeited ticket.

stops.title: Alcatraz Day Tour, Pier 33
stops.notes: $47.95 adult on the day tour. The only rule that matters: tickets release 90 days ahead on alcatrazcitycruises.com and you buy them the morning they drop. Summer sailings are gone four to six weeks out; night tours go faster still. Alcatraz City Cruises is the only operator the Park Service authorises, so every third-party Alcatraz package is either the same ticket with a markup or a boat that circles the island and never lands. On the rock: the cellhouse audio tour is 45 minutes and is the best thing on the island, then the agave trail and the gardens. Two and a half hours is right; take the 13:50 back. Bring a real layer — mid-bay is ten degrees colder than the Embarcadero and windier than you have planned for.

stops.title: Late lunch at Tony's Pizza Napoletana
stops.notes: Twelve pizza styles on one menu, but only 73 Margherita pizzas a day — that one comes out of the 900-degree wood oven and they stop when the dough runs out, usually early evening. Coming off the 13:50 boat and eating at 14:45 is the whole trick: no reservations for parties under six, and the 18:30 wait is 90 minutes on the sidewalk.

stops.title: City Lights, then a drink at Vesuvio across the alley
stops.notes: The Poetry Room is upstairs and the window bench is the point of the visit. Vesuvio is directly across Jack Kerouac Alley, has been pouring since 1948, and serves no food — which is why you ate first. Caffe Trieste two blocks up if you would rather have coffee than a drink.

stops.title: Filbert Steps up to Coit Tower
stops.notes: Climb the wooden Filbert Steps from Sansome — cottage gardens, the wild parrots, and no parking problem, because the Coit Tower lot is a 40-minute crawl that people sit in rather than walk ten minutes. The 1934 WPA murals in the base are free to look at; the fee is only the elevator to the observation deck, and the view from the terrace outside costs nothing and is almost the same.

stops.title: Salt-and-pepper crab at R&G Lounge
stops.notes: Book the upstairs room; the ground floor is walk-in chaos with a queue on Kearny. Order the salt-and-pepper crab — market price, usually $50-60 for a whole one, and it is the dish the entire restaurant is built around — plus greens and rice, and stop there. Ten minutes downhill from Coit Tower through the Chinatown alleys, which is the right way to arrive.

playbooks.name: The Mission: Tartine at nine, Balmy Alley with a muralist, and settling the burrito argument
playbooks.summary: The warmest, sunniest neighbourhood in San Francisco done on foot in the order that beats its queues — bakery before the line, the 1776 adobe before the tour buses, murals with somebody who paints them, and two taquerias two blocks apart that people will fight about.

sourceTrip.name: California, two weeks, no freeway if we can help it

stops.title: Morning bun at Tartine, before the line exists
stops.notes: At 08:45 the queue at 18th and Guerrero is five minutes; by 09:30 it is twenty and by 11:00 it is forty-five. Order the morning bun and a hot croissant and skip the bread — the country loaf comes out of the oven around 16:30 and you are not carrying it around all day. Tartine Manufactory on Alabama has tables and no line and is not the same thing.

stops.title: Mission Dolores — the adobe, not the basilica

location.name: Mission San Francisco de Asis (Mission Dolores)

stops.notes: $10 suggested donation. The small adobe chapel on the left is 1776 and the oldest intact building in San Francisco; the enormous basilica beside it is 1918 and you can walk past it. Look up in the chapel — the ceiling is original Ohlone painted work, not a restoration. Twenty minutes is enough, and the cemetery behind it is the one from Vertigo.

stops.title: Dolores Park, north-west slope
stops.notes: The slope facing downtown catches sun an hour before the rest of the park and is the corner locals sit on. More usefully: if the Sunset and the Richmond are socked in, the Mission is often clear — it sits in the city's rain and fog shadow and is reliably its warmest neighbourhood. That, not the murals, is the reason to schedule a walking day here rather than in Golden Gate Park.

stops.title: Precita Eyes classic mural walk
stops.notes: $25 general, $15 seniors, $10 under 18. Weekends only, leaving from 2981 24th Street near Harrison. This is the rare guided walk worth paying for: a working muralist covers 60 to 70 murals inside six blocks and tells you which walls are being repainted, by whom, and over what. Book ahead — the groups are small and there is one guide.

stops.title: Balmy Alley again, slowly, with nobody talking
stops.notes: Walk it a second time on your own after the tour. It is the oldest continuous mural site in the city — the first panels went up in 1971 and the dense 1980s Central America wall is the heart of it. Several of those are being restored by the original artists on a 2026 grant, so what is on the wall now is not what is in the guidebook photograph. It is a working alley with garages and residents; go quietly and do not shoot into windows.

stops.title: The burrito argument: La Taqueria versus El Farolito
stops.notes: They are two blocks apart on Mission Street and the argument is genuine. La Taqueria at 2889 makes it with no rice — dorado, griddled until the tortilla crisps — and the absence of rice is the position, not an oversight. El Farolito at 2779 is the super burrito: cash only, foil the length of a forearm, open until 02:00, and the one the after-hours crowd votes for. If there are two of you, buy one of each and split them. Do not walk in and ask for a Mission burrito; it is a category, not a menu item, and nobody behind the counter will know what you mean.

stops.title: Dandelion Chocolate on Valencia
stops.notes: A bean-to-bar factory with a cafe bolted to the front of it; the hot chocolate flight is three small cups from three origins and is far more interesting than buying a bar. If you would rather read than eat, Adobe Books and Alley Cat Books are both within three blocks and both host readings most weeknights.

stops.title: Dinner in the courtyard at Foreign Cinema
stops.notes: Ask for the courtyard when you book, not the dining room — a film runs on the back wall through service and the heaters make April work. Two weeks out for a Friday or Saturday. The brunch here is more famous and much harder to get; dinner is the easier and better meal.

playbooks.name: Lands End to Fort Point: ruins at low tide, the Coastal Trail, and standing under the bridge
playbooks.summary: The free day. Sutro Baths before the lot fills, the cypress trail along the cliff, across to the Presidio for lunch over the tunnels, and Fort Point in the afternoon — a Civil War brick fort the Golden Gate Bridge was re-engineered to spare. Under $100 and the best walking in the city.

sourceTrip.name: Pacific edge: San Francisco to San Diego

stops.title: Sutro Baths ruins, at low water
stops.notes: Free, and the lot above the ruins holds about 75 cars and is full by 10:00 on any clear day — 08:15 is the entire trick, and the overflow is a half-mile of El Camino del Mar. Check a tide table before you commit: at low water you can walk the concrete tanks and into the cave on the north side; at high water the cave floods, the surge comes over the sill and people get hurt in it every year. June mornings here are fogged in until 11:00 and the ruins are better for it.

stops.title: Lands End Coastal Trail to Eagle's Point
stops.notes: 3.4 miles out and back on the bed of an old railway, so it is flatter than the cliff makes it look. Two detours are the reason to walk it rather than drive to the viewpoint: the steps down from Mile Rock Overlook to the stone labyrinth on the headland, and the shipwreck view at low tide below Painted Rock. Paved and wheelchair-accessible as far as Mile Rock; stairs beyond that.

stops.title: Legion of Honor, if the fog holds
stops.notes: $20 adult, free to Bay Area residents on Saturdays and to everyone on the first Tuesday of the month. Worth it for the Rodin court and the building itself, which sits on a golf-course bluff with the bridge behind it. Marked as an idea on purpose: if the marine layer has burned off by 11:00, skip it without a second thought — the rest of this day is outside and the museum will still be there in fog.

stops.title: The 29 bus across to the Presidio
stops.notes: The 29 Sunset runs from Lands End into the Presidio without a transfer, about 35 minutes. The free PresidiGo shuttle is only useful once you are already inside the park, and it does not come out to the ocean. Driving works too, but then you give up the parking space you queued for at 08:15.

stops.title: Lunch on the Tunnel Tops
stops.notes: Fourteen acres of new parkland laid directly over the Doyle Drive tunnels, with the bridge straight ahead. The Tunnel Tops themselves sell nothing — buy food at the Transit Center picnic area below or on the Main Post and carry it up, which is the mistake everyone makes once. The Field Station tables at the west end are the ones with the view.

stops.title: Battery Bluff, then down to Crissy Field
stops.notes: The newest piece of the Presidio and almost always empty: four restored coastal gun batteries on a bluff that most of the city drives underneath without knowing. From there it is a mile downhill past the marsh to Crissy Field and the Warming Hut, which is the last coffee before the fort.

stops.title: Fort Point, under the south anchorage
stops.notes: Free — and open Friday to Sunday only, 10:00 to 17:00. Turning up on a Tuesday is by a distance the most common way this day fails, so check the NPS page the week you go. It is a Civil War brick casemate fort that Joseph Strauss threw a steel arch over rather than demolish, which is why the bridge has that arch at all. Go to the third-floor gallery and then the roof: you stand directly beneath the span with the deck humming above you. The wind funnelling through the Gate here is genuinely punishing — this is the layer you have been carrying since Sutro.

stops.title: Burmese on Clement Street
stops.notes: No reservations, ever — put your name on the list, walk two blocks for a beer, come back when they text. Tea leaf salad tossed at the table and the coconut rice is the order. If the wait is over an hour, Good Luck Dim Sum three blocks up is cash only, about $3 a plate, and shuts at 18:30 — so decide fast. Clement Street is the reason the Inner Richmond is called the second Chinatown and it is a better dinner street than anywhere near the bridge.

playbooks.name: Napa done properly: Schramsberg caves, Frog's Leap, Stag's Leap — and somebody else driving
playbooks.summary: Three appointment-only tastings north to south with a real sit-down lunch wedged in the middle and a hired car for the day, because you cannot legally or safely do this valley on your own. About $480 a head and that is the honest number, not the padded one.

sourceTrip.name: Wine country, the year we finally booked ahead

stops.title: Coffee downtown before the car comes
stops.notes: Eat something solid now. Three tastings is roughly fifteen pours, the first one is at 10:00, and lunch is not until 12:15 — the people who skip this are the people who are finished by the third appointment.

stops.title: Car and driver for the day
stops.notes: This is not a luxury, it is the thing that makes the day possible. Three appointments are spread over 25 miles of Highway 29 and the Silverado Trail, and Napa County polices that exact road on that exact day extremely hard. A full-day private car runs $650-$1,500 per group — typically $85-$200 an hour with a five- or six-hour minimum, plus 18-20% gratuity — and the figure here is one seat of four in a $780 day including tip. Book two to three weeks ahead in harvest season. A driver also knows which tasting rooms will hold a case for you until the end of the day and which will not, which matters more than it sounds.

stops.title: Schramsberg: two miles of 1870s caves
stops.notes: $75 for the cave tour and tasting, appointment only, and it books weeks out — this is not a place you walk into, and neither are the other two. Start here because it is the northern end of the valley and because the tunnels sit at about 55F, which is the coldest thing you will do today: take a jacket in with you. Hand-dug by Chinese labourers in the 1870s and stacked floor to ceiling with riddled bottles. Sparkling first is also the right order for your palate.

stops.title: A real lunch at Farmstead
stops.notes: Ninety minutes, sitting down, with actual food. This is the stop people cut to fit a fourth winery in and then regret at 16:00. Book it — the old nursery barn fills at weekends. Gott's Roadside is directly across Highway 29 and is the $20 version if you would rather put the money in the glass.

stops.title: Frog's Leap, in the garden if they will have you
stops.notes: $40-55 by reservation, in a red barn surrounded by an organic kitchen garden. Dry-farmed and certified organic since decades before either became a marketing line, and they will genuinely talk you through why the vines get no irrigation and what that does to the fruit. Ask for the garden tasting when you book; the barn is the wet-weather fallback. Deliberately the middle appointment — it is the most relaxed hour of the day and you want it between the caves and the cabernet.

stops.title: Stag's Leap Wine Cellars on the Silverado Trail
stops.notes: $75-125 depending which estate flight you book; pay the top of the range and taste the FAY and S.L.V. blocks side by side, which is the actual reason to come — this is the cabernet that won the 1976 Paris tasting. Last of the three on purpose: it is the biggest wine and the southern end of the valley, so the run back to town is fifteen minutes. Do not try to add a fourth. Three appointments plus a proper lunch is the honest ceiling for one day and everyone who has tried four has told the same story about it afterwards.

stops.title: Oxbow Public Market before it shuts
stops.notes: Oysters at Hog Island, a Model Bakery English muffin to take back for the morning, and something salty to finish on after a day of tannin. Most stalls close at 19:00, so this only works if the last tasting ran to time.

playbooks.name: The Russian River instead: two great pinots, a picnic, and half the money
playbooks.summary: The wine day Napa's neighbours do better — appointment-only pinot, a sandwich from a grocery, and nobody in a queue.

sourceTrip.name: California, two weeks, no freeway if we can help it

stops.title: Coffee on the Healdsburg plaza
stops.notes: Park on the plaza once and leave the car there until you pick up the driver. Healdsburg's free two-hour spots are enforced and the lots behind the plaza are not obvious from the square.

stops.title: Driver picks up — Westside Road
stops.notes: The same rule as Napa and for the same reason, but a third of the cost: Russian River tasting rooms are 15 minutes apart instead of 25, so a four-hour booking covers the day. Split four ways this is $60 a head. If you are two people, the honest alternative is one taster and one driver, which nobody enjoys.

stops.title: Rochioli, on the terrace
stops.notes: Continuously family-run since the 1930s, and the 1985 estate pinot is the wine that told America the Russian River could do this. The tasting room is small and the terrace looks straight down the vineyard rows — go here first, while your palate is clean and the room is empty.

stops.title: Merry Edwards, the pinot flight
stops.notes: $75 for the seated flight, and the fee is waived against a three-bottle purchase — which is worth knowing before you decide it is expensive. Book it; walk-ins are not a thing here.

stops.title: Lunch out of a grocery store
stops.notes: The move nobody tells you: Sonoma's best wine lunch is a sandwich and a peach from a proper grocery, eaten at a picnic table at the next winery. It costs a fifth of a vineyard restaurant and it is the reason this day is half the price of the Napa one.

stops.title: Dry Creek Vineyard, in the shade
stops.notes: A third tasting is where a wine day usually goes wrong. This one works because it is a different valley and a different grape — old-vine zinfandel after two pinots — so your palate has something to do.

stops.title: Back to the plaza, and a swim in the river if it is warm
stops.notes: Between June and September the dam turns this stretch into a swimming beach with a lifeguard. In January it is a gravel bar and a heron, which is also fine.

stops.title: Dinner at the Matheson, upstairs
stops.notes: The wine wall upstairs pours 88 Sonoma wines by the glass in three sizes, which is the correct end to a day when you have already had three tastings and do not want a bottle.

playbooks.name: Capitola in the morning, West Cliff at sunset, and the cable car down to dinner
playbooks.summary: The Monterey Bay's other side — a pastel village, a warm-water swim, and the surfers at Steamer Lane.

sourceTrip.name: Bay Area, the long weekend that became a week

stops.title: Breakfast at Gayle's, ordered at the back
stops.notes: Two queues and everybody joins the wrong one. Pastries and coffee are the front counter; the hot case at the back is where the actual breakfast is, and it moves faster.

stops.title: Capitola Village and the wharf
stops.notes: The wharf reopened after a long rebuild — the storm that took the middle out of it in 2023 is why the timber is two colours. Walk to the end for the only view that puts the pastel Venetian cottages and the cliffs in one frame.

stops.title: Swim at Capitola Beach
stops.notes: The genuinely useful fact about this coast: Capitola sits in a south-facing pocket, so the water is several degrees warmer and the wind is far softer than anywhere on the open coast. This is the swim that is actually pleasant without a wetsuit.

stops.title: Lunch on the sand at Zelda's
stops.notes: Right on the sand and priced for it. If the wait is over twenty minutes, walk two doors to Pete's and eat sooner for less.

stops.title: Drive West Cliff, park at Lighthouse Point
stops.notes: Ten minutes up the coast. Do the drive rather than the Boardwalk unless you have children with you — West Cliff is the reason people live here and the Boardwalk is a car park with a rollercoaster attached.

stops.title: Steamer Lane from the cliff

location.name: Steamer Lane, Lighthouse Field State Beach

stops.notes: You watch this one from above, which is rare and is what makes it worth the stop — the cliff at Lighthouse Point puts you directly over the takeoff. The Surfing Museum in the lighthouse itself is one room and twenty minutes.

stops.title: Natural Bridges at golden hour
stops.notes: $10 a vehicle. Between October and January the eucalyptus grove behind the beach holds an overwintering monarch colony, which is a completely different reason to come and is signposted from the car park.

stops.title: Dinner at Shadowbrook, down the cable car
stops.notes: Open since 1947, and you descend to it in a hillside funicular through a garden — which sounds like a gimmick and is the best twenty seconds of the evening. Book the cable-car level rather than the Rock Room. If you are staying within three miles they will send a 1966 Checker cab for you.

playbooks.name: The Aquarium's first forty minutes, the Lone Cypress, and a long dinner in Carmel
playbooks.summary: One coast road, three things it is famous for, and the ticket rule that makes the toll disappear.

sourceTrip.name: California, two weeks, no freeway if we can help it

stops.title: Coffee, then park at the Aquarium end of Cannery Row
stops.notes: The Aquarium does not sell tickets at the door — they are online only, and the 10:00 slot is the one to hold. Park in a Cannery Row garage rather than circling: the street spots near the Aquarium are two-hour and this is a three-hour visit.

stops.title: Monterey Bay Aquarium, at opening
stops.notes: $65, open 10:00-17:00 daily. The first forty minutes are the whole trick — go straight past the entrance exhibits to the Kelp Forest and the Open Sea while everybody else is still in the lobby, then work backwards. By 11:30 those two rooms are three deep.

stops.title: The 17-Mile Drive gate
stops.notes: $12.25 per vehicle, cash or card at the gate. Enter at Pacific Grove rather than Carmel and you drive the coast section with the ocean on your right and the pull-outs on your side of the road.

stops.title: Lunch at the Bench, inside the gate

location.name: The Bench, The Lodge at Pebble Beach

stops.notes: This is the stop that pays for itself. The 17-Mile Drive gate is $12.25 a vehicle and the fee is refunded against a $35-or-more bill at any Pebble Beach Resorts restaurant — but NOT the market, so a sandwich at the deli does not count. Keep the gate receipt and hand it over with the bill.

stops.title: Bird Rock, the Lone Cypress, Ghost Trees
stops.notes: Three pull-outs are worth stopping at and the other fourteen are not. Bird Rock for the noise, the Lone Cypress because you came for it, and the bleached Ghost Trees at Pescadero Point, which nobody photographs and should.

stops.title: Carmel-by-the-Sea on foot
stops.notes: The town has no street numbers, so every address is a corner and a courtyard — 'Dolores between 5th and 6th' is a real address, not somebody being vague. The galleries and passageways off Ocean Avenue are the point; the beach at the bottom of the hill is the sunset.

stops.title: Carmel Beach for sunset
stops.notes: White sand, cypress, and dogs off-lead everywhere — this is one of the few California beaches where that is the rule rather than an infraction. Fires are allowed south of 10th Avenue only.

stops.title: Dinner at Aubergine
stops.notes: The tasting menu, and the reason this day costs what it does. Book it a month out; it is a small room and there is one seating. The wine pairing is the honest half of the bill and worth taking.

playbooks.name: Big Sur in December: Bixby at first light, the keyhole at four, and a room on the cliff
playbooks.summary: The one time of year the Pfeiffer keyhole lights — and the day built around getting there for it.

sourceTrip.name: California, two weeks, no freeway if we can help it

stops.title: Check Highway 1 before you turn the key
stops.notes: Not optional, and not a formality. Highway 1 reopened through Big Sur in January 2026 after years of slip closures, and by that August the Timber Fire had shut it again from the San Luis Obispo county line to north of Sand Dollar. The northern half — Bixby to Julia Pfeiffer Burns — is the part this day uses, but the closure line moves. Ten minutes on QuickMap decides whether today is this day or a different one.

stops.title: Bixby Creek Bridge before the light is up
stops.notes: Fifteen miles south of Carmel and the reason to leave in the dark. Park in the pull-out on the north side and walk back onto Old Coast Road for the angle everybody recognises. By ten there are forty cars and a queue for it.

stops.title: Point Sur Light Station from the road
stops.notes: The lighthouse itself only opens for guided walks on set days, so treat it as a viewpoint unless you have booked one. The volcanic rock it sits on is the best-looking thing on this stretch and costs nothing to look at.

stops.title: The redwoods at Pfeiffer Big Sur
stops.notes: $10 a vehicle. The Valley View and Buzzard's Roost trails are here, and they matter on this day for a specific reason: you need somewhere to be for six hours before the light is right at the beach, and this is the only place on the coast with shade, water and a lavatory.

stops.title: Lunch at Nepenthe, on the terrace
stops.notes: Open since 1949 and still the best 800 feet of view you can buy with a hamburger. No reservations — put your name in and wait at the fire pit, which is the intended experience rather than a failure of one. The Phoenix shop below it is where the queue actually goes.

stops.title: McWay Falls at Julia Pfeiffer Burns
stops.notes: An eighty-foot waterfall onto a beach you are not allowed to walk on, seen from a quarter-mile paved trail through a tunnel under the highway. Park in the lot rather than the highway shoulder — the shoulder here is a genuine hazard and is ticketed.

stops.title: Pfeiffer Beach, for the keyhole
stops.notes: The whole reason this day is dated in December. Sunset light only passes through Keyhole Rock for a few weeks either side of the solstice, when the sun sets far enough south — come in July and you get a nice beach and no beam. Sycamore Canyon Road is two miles of single track with no sign on Highway 1 (it is the only paved left turn between the Big Sur post office and Nepenthe), a gate that shuts at sunset, and a cash kiosk. The purple sand is real; it is manganese garnet washing out of the cliff.

stops.title: A room at Post Ranch, and dinner at Sierra Mar
stops.notes: The honest number: rooms start around $2,175 a night and January weeknights average more, so this is roughly $1,090 a head for two and it is the single most expensive stop in this whole library. What you are buying is a cliff-edge room with no television and the Sierra Mar dining room, which is open to non-guests by reservation only if you would rather have the dinner and sleep in Carmel — that version of this day costs a tenth as much and loses only the morning.
